title: Civilization Detectives: Geography Shapes Choices
subject: social-studies
learningObjective: Use geographic evidence to explain how rivers, landforms, climate, and resources influenced an ancient civilization's choices.
successCriteria: I can locate the key physical features on a map.
I can distinguish a geographic fact from an inference.
I can explain one way geography created an opportunity or constraint.
I can support a historical claim with at least two connected pieces of evidence.
essentialQuestion: How can a map help us explain why people built communities where they did?

quiz.question: Which statement is a map fact?
choices: A river appears along the eastern edge of the map.
The river made every decision for the people.
The settlement was definitely peaceful.
The people chose the best possible site.
quiz.correctAnswer: A river appears along the eastern edge of the map.
quiz.explanation: A map fact describes evidence directly visible in the source.

quiz.question: How can a river be both an opportunity and a constraint?
choices: It can support farming but also flood nearby land.
It has only benefits.
It has only problems.
It cannot affect people.
quiz.correctAnswer: It can support farming but also flood nearby land.
quiz.explanation: Historical reasoning considers connected benefits and tradeoffs.

quiz.question: What is a historical inference?
choices: A conclusion supported by evidence and reasoning.
A map symbol copied without explanation.
A guess that needs no evidence.
A list of directions.
quiz.correctAnswer: A conclusion supported by evidence and reasoning.
quiz.explanation: An inference goes beyond the visible fact but must still be grounded in evidence.

quiz.question: Why should a settlement-site claim use more than one map clue?
choices: Multiple connected clues make the explanation more defensible.
Maps always require exactly two clues.
One clue is never true.
More clues make an answer automatically correct.
quiz.correctAnswer: Multiple connected clues make the explanation more defensible.
quiz.explanation: Two or more relevant clues can show a stronger cause-and-effect explanation.

quiz.question: A student says a civilization formed beside a river only because the river was nearby. What is missing?
choices: An explanation of what the river enabled or made difficult.
A new map title.
A longer sentence with no evidence.
A list of unrelated cities.
quiz.correctAnswer: An explanation of what the river enabled or made difficult.
quiz.explanation: The learner must connect the feature to a human opportunity, constraint, or choice.

quiz.question: What should you inspect first when a map symbol is confusing?
choices: The map legend or key.
The map border only.
A random location.
The answer choices before the map.
quiz.explanation: The legend explains what symbols and patterns represent.

quiz.question: Which claim is most defensible?
choices: The river guaranteed that the civilization would become powerful.
The river may have supported farming and travel, while flooding created a risk.
The river caused every cultural belief.
The map proves what every person thought.
quiz.correctAnswer: The river may have supported farming and travel, while flooding created a risk.
quiz.explanation: A careful claim connects evidence to likely effects without pretending one factor explains everything.

quiz.question: Explain one way a landform could shape a settlement choice.
quiz.correctAnswer: A response names a landform and explains a supported opportunity or constraint it created.
quiz.explanation: The answer should connect a physical feature to a human choice with evidence.

quiz.question: Which statement is an unsupported inference?
choices: The map shows a road near the settlement.
The road may have helped movement because it connects the settlement to other areas.
The people who used the road were happier than everyone else.
The settlement is near a water source shown in the legend.
quiz.correctAnswer: The people who used the road were happier than everyone else.
quiz.explanation: The map does not provide evidence for a claim about people’s feelings.

quiz.question: When comparing two settlement sites, what should a historian do?
choices: Name evidence, explain tradeoffs, and defend a conclusion.
Choose the site with the most attractive name.
Count only the map colors.
Assume the larger site is always better.
quiz.correctAnswer: Name evidence, explain tradeoffs, and defend a conclusion.
quiz.explanation: Comparison requires evidence-based judgment rather than a surface preference.

knowledge: Physical geography includes features and resources that shape the choices available to communities.
capability: Read a map and construct a geography-to-choice explanation.
reasoning: Weigh multiple geographic factors instead of treating one feature as a complete explanation.
retention: Retrieve the fact-versus-inference distinction and opportunity-constraint pair after a delay.
transfer: Apply the map-evidence method to a different ancient or modern settlement.

visual.title: Civilization map lab
visual.caption: Physical feature -> opportunity or constraint -> community choice
visual.altText: A map evidence model connects a river valley, landform, climate, or resource to an opportunity or constraint and then to a settlement choice.

visualSupports.title: The civilization map lab
visualSupports.description: A layered map shows a river, floodplain, mountains, desert, and settlement sites.
visualSupports.altText: A map with a river valley, mountains, desert, resources, and a settlement marked.

visualSupports.title: Feature to choice chain
visualSupports.description: An arrow diagram connects a physical feature to an opportunity or constraint and then to a human choice.
visualSupports.altText: Physical feature leads to opportunity or constraint, which leads to a community choice.

visualSupports.title: Map fact or historical inference?
visualSupports.description: Cards distinguish what the map directly shows from what a historian cautiously infers.
visualSupports.altText: Two labeled columns compare map facts and historical inferences.

phaseModules.title: Open the map lab
phaseModules.studentAction: Study the settlement map and predict one reason the community formed there. Mark the evidence that made you think it.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can separate my first idea from the evidence I noticed.

phaseModules.title: Trace geography to a choice
phaseModules.studentAction: Follow one example from river access to farming opportunity, then to a community decision.
phaseModules.successCheck: The explanation names the feature, its effect, and the choice.

phaseModules.title: Fact, inference, or guess?
phaseModules.studentAction: Sort map statements into directly shown facts, reasonable inferences, and unsupported guesses.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can explain what evidence an inference still needs.

phaseModules.title: Build a geography evidence card
phaseModules.studentAction: Choose two map features, label each as an opportunity or constraint, and connect them to a likely community choice.
phaseModules.successCheck: Both features connect to the choice without inventing evidence.

phaseModules.title: Debate the best site
phaseModules.studentAction: Compare two possible settlement sites and defend which is stronger using a river, landform, climate, or resource claim.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can acknowledge a tradeoff and still defend my conclusion.

phaseModules.title: Explain a civilization choice
phaseModules.studentAction: Write a claim explaining why a community formed where it did, then cite two map clues and connect each clue to the claim.
phaseModules.successCheck: The explanation distinguishes evidence from inference.

phaseModules.title: Retrieve the map reasoning loop
phaseModules.studentAction: After a delay, recall feature -> opportunity or constraint -> choice, and classify one fact and one inference.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can use the loop without seeing the original map.

phaseModules.title: Investigate a new settlement
phaseModules.studentAction: Use a new map of an ancient or modern settlement to make and revise a geography-based explanation.
phaseModules.successCheck: The reasoning method survives a different place and time.

phaseModules.title: Choose the next historian move
phaseModules.studentAction: If the map reading is weak, return to the legend; if the cause is weak, trace the arrow; if evidence is weak, find a second connected feature.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can identify the exact part of my historical explanation to repair.

proofTasks.prompt: Explain the difference between a map fact and a historical inference.
Explain how one physical feature can create both an opportunity and a constraint.
Defend a settlement-site claim from a new map using two evidence points.
Complete a delayed feature-to-choice retrieval check.
Apply map evidence to explain a different settlement pattern.

feedbackRules.result: The learner names what the map shows but does not explain its effect.
feedbackRules.hint: Ask: What did this feature make easier or harder?

feedbackRules.result: One geographic feature is treated as the entire explanation.
feedbackRules.hint: Find a second feature and identify a tradeoff.

feedbackRules.result: The conclusion goes beyond what the evidence can support.
feedbackRules.hint: Label the statement as a guess, then name the missing evidence.
feedbackRules.action: Route to fact-inference sorting and revise.

reteachPaths.trigger: The learner cannot connect a map feature to a human choice.
reteachPaths.action: Use one labeled map feature, one opportunity-or-constraint card, and one sentence frame before returning to the full site comparison.

prerequisiteRepairPaths.trigger: The learner cannot read the legend or identify map features.
prerequisiteRepairPaths.action: Repair legend, direction, and symbol reading with a short map scavenger hunt.

challengePaths.trigger: The learner supports a site claim with connected evidence.
challengePaths.action: Compare two civilizations and explain how similar geographic features produced different choices.

commonMisunderstandings: A map fact automatically proves a cause.
Ancient people chose sites for only one reason.
parentTeacherNotes: Keep the distinction between evidence and inference explicit. Historical explanations should be cautious and multi-causal.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a text description and tactile or keyboard version of the map.
Use labels and patterns in addition to color.
Accept spoken, typed, or annotated-map evidence.
